title: China's new cyberspace inspection rules take effect — and formally include AI
subtitle: The Ministry of Public Security's October 1 measures replace an eight-year-old framework and give police inspection authority over algorithm recommendation governance, training data, and AI ethics compliance for the first time.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: China's Measures for Public Security Organs' Supervision and Inspection of Cyberspace Security came into force on October 1, 2026, replacing the 2018 Provisions on Internet Security Supervision and Inspection. The new measures expand the Ministry of Public Security's inspection authority across eleven categories: network access filing, internal security management, user registration and log retention, multi-level protection scheme compliance, Critical Information Infrastructure safeguards, intrusion and malware defenses, vulnerability remediation, content controls, algorithm recommendation governance, data and personal information protection, and cooperation with national-security investigations. For the first time, AI is explicitly within scope — a new article in the amended Cybersecurity Law directs the state to support AI innovation while strengthening ethics regulation and risk assessment.

This changes who can walk into an AI company and ask to see the training data. Under the 2018 framework, inspections targeted traditional network operators. The 2026 measures put algorithm recommendation systems and AI services on the same inspection list as critical infrastructure, with the Ministry of Public Security — not just the Cyberspace Administration — as the inspecting agency. The practical effect is that model providers operating in China now face compliance checks on their algorithms, their training-data provenance, and their user-logging practices, with police authority behind the request.

China's approach is now visibly distinct from both the US and the EU. The EU AI Act, which hit full effect on August 2, 2026, works through documentation, conformity assessments, and administrative penalties. The US is layering FTC consumer-protection authority on top of voluntary commitments like last week's White House super-intelligence accord. China is using police inspection authority. The three regimes will all shape the same models — any frontier lab operating globally will have to satisfy all three at once — and the differences in enforcement style will drive different design choices about logging, data retention, and content filtering.

For learners thinking about compliance careers in AI: the three-regime split is going to define the next five years of AI governance work. If you can read an EU AI Act Annex alongside an MPS inspection checklist alongside an FTC consent decree, you are in a small group. Pick one jurisdiction, read its live rules — the actual effective ones, not the drafts — and track one real enforcement action through to conclusion. That is more useful than any introductory course on AI policy.
